title: When Buckminster Fuller Proposed Putting a Dome Over Manhattan (1960)

body:
in Architecture, History |   	October 1st, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			
Image via Buck­min­ster Fuller Estate
The nov­els of John Brun­ner have become a niche taste, even with­in his genre of sci­ence fic­tion. A more soci­o­log­i­cal­ly mind­ed ver­sion of Philip K. Dick at his best, he could write with what now looks like a simul­ta­ne­ous pre­science about the civ­i­liza­tion to come and an apoc­a­lyp­ti­cal­ly anx­ious con­cern with the issues of his day. His undis­put­ed mas­ter­piece Stand on Zanz­ibar came out in 1968, the same year as the late Paul R. Ehrlich’s The Pop­u­la­tion Bomb. Both books deal with the dire con­se­quences of what, at the time, looked like the run­away mul­ti­pli­ca­tion of human­i­ty, though ele­ments of the dystopi­an sci-fi writer’s vision now look rather more cred­i­ble than the pre­dic­tions of the Stan­ford biol­o­gist — apart from the giant geo­des­ic dome cov­er­ing Man­hat­tan, any­way.
In a sense, Brun­ner was actu­al­ly behind the times, since Buck­min­ster Fuller him­self had sug­gest­ed dom­ing Man­hat­tan near­ly a decade ear­li­er. In their ambi­tious pro­pos­al for a “two-mile-wide Dome Over Man­hat­tan” from the turn of the nine­teen-six­ties, Fuller and long­time col­lab­o­ra­tor Sho­ji Sadao “imag­ined a mas­sive archi­tec­tur­al sur­face that would reg­u­late the city’s ecosys­tems,” write Next City’s Janette Kim and Erik Carv­er. “They deliv­ered this design along with a series of sur­pris­ing cal­cu­la­tions: the Dome would reduce heat loss by scal­ing the city to one eighty-fifth of its sur­face area; the elim­i­na­tion of snow­plow­ing alone would pay for heat; build­ings inside the Dome could be built lighter and cheap­er with­out need for weath­er­proof­ing; and inte­ri­or air could be heat­ed by remote plants.”
Fuller and Sadao did bring some num­bers to back up their claims, but even more impor­tant­ly, they made assur­ances that the dome’s glass would be one-way, a defense against pry­ing non-Man­hat­tan­ite eyes, and would keep res­i­dents’ cars and lawns in prime con­di­tion. How­ev­er out­landish­ly for­ward-think­ing Fuller could be, he nev­er for­got that he need­ed to appeal to the wor­ries and aspi­ra­tions of mid-cen­tu­ry Amer­i­ca. As a per­son­al­i­ty, he also fit in well with the era’s enthu­si­asm for sweep­ing infra­struc­tur­al fix­es. “It was a time when peo­ple real­ly believed in the pow­er of tech­nol­o­gy,” says Nev­er Built New York co-author Sam Lubell. “We’re build­ing space­ships that go to the moon. Why can’t we build a dome over Man­hat­tan to get rid of all this pol­lu­tion, get rid of all the prob­lems of weath­er?”
Still, as eccen­tric as he was, Fuller was­n’t delu­sion­al. “It’d be very worth­while to have cities under geo­des­ic domes, but New York City, if you think about all the dif­fer­ent own­ers of dif­fer­ent lands, the con­tro­ver­sy about ‘this is my air rights, I don’t want a thing over my thing here,’ I just don’t think it’s going to hap­pen,” he admit­ted. But “it can hap­pen where you start out in places where ener­gy is a real­ly fan­tas­tic prob­lem.” At the time, the ever-increas­ing demand for resources of all kinds by a rapid­ly grow­ing pop­u­la­tion appeared to be not just a but the fan­tas­tic prob­lem. Today, once-unfore­see­able devel­op­ments like ris­ing ener­gy effi­cien­cy and an appar­ent­ly inex­orable decline in glob­al birthrates have direct­ed our ner­vous gazes else­where. Yet dat­ed visions of tech­no­log­i­cal utopia and dystopia still strike us as odd­ly famil­iar — and indeed, as strange­ly sim­i­lar to one anoth­er.

Based in Seoul, Col­in Marshall writes and broad­casts on cities, lan­guage, and cul­ture. He’s the author of the newslet­ter Books on Cities as well as the books 한국 요약 금지 (No Sum­ma­riz­ing Korea) and Kore­an Newtro. Fol­low him on the social net­work for­mer­ly known as Twit­ter at @colinmarshall.

title: LEGO Lets You Build Gaudí’s Sagrada Família in Its Largest Set Ever

body:
in Architecture |   	October 1st, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

When work on the Sagra­da Família first began in 1882, the orig­i­nal archi­tect could hard­ly have imag­ined that, 144 years lat­er, the ambi­tious under­tak­ing would still be under­way. Yet here we are. Famous­ly, the Cata­lan archi­tect Antoni Gaudí (1852–1926) spent the last four decades of his life design­ing and build­ing the Goth­ic-inspired basil­i­ca in Barcelona. Then came the Span­ish Civ­il War (1936–1939), which destroyed many of his archi­tec­tur­al plans, leav­ing suc­ces­sive gen­er­a­tions of archi­tects to piece togeth­er Gaudí’s vision and move the project for­ward. At long last, ear­li­er this year, builders com­plet­ed the cen­tral Tow­er of Jesus Christ, which stands 566 feet high, mak­ing the Sagra­da Família the tallest church in the world.
Although work on the Glo­ry façade still remains, the basil­i­ca has reached a near-com­plete state—complete enough for Lego to roll out the offi­cial Sagra­da Família Lego set. At 12,060 pieces, it’s the largest Lego set ever made, and it lets you build the Sagra­da Família sec­tion by sec­tion, fol­low­ing the same order as the orig­i­nal archi­tects. “Your build­ing jour­ney begins with the Apse with Crypt, the Nativ­i­ty façade and the Pas­sion façade. It then moves on to the naves and the West­ern Sac­risty. Com­plete the 6 tow­ers and fin­ish the basil­i­ca with the East­ern Sac­risty and the Glo­ry façade.” With the video above, you can watch the build­ing of the Lego basil­i­ca, com­press­ing hours of work into 10 min­utes. The Lego set will be avail­able on Novem­ber 1, 2026.
via Kot­tke

title: Gaia Alari's Lilting Animations are Drawn Frame by Frame
description: Gaia Alari’s works are defined by a distinct, effervescent visual language. Made from thousands of handmade drawings on paper, the artist’s elabor
body:
Gaia Alari’s works are defined by a distinct, effervescent visual language. Made from thousands of handmade drawings on paper, the artist’s elaborate animations put on strikingly tactile performances as fleeting marks of oil pastel and charcoal dance across the screen.
Meandering botanical forms, gestural bodies, and sweeping birds converge into fluid loops that create a rhythm reminiscent of a stream of consciousness. Whether Alari is collaborating with a brand, exploring personal interests, or creating static illustrations, it’s clear that each piece tells a distinct story. Watch more from the artist on Vimeo and keep up with her explorations on Instagram.

title: World of WearableArt's 'GLO!' Is a Celebration of Culture, Nature, and Whimsy
description: Avant-garde style, technology, and performance converge in a fantastical, joyous competition every year in New Zealand. World of WearableArt is a
body:
Avant-garde style, technology, and performance converge in a fantastical, joyous competition every year in New Zealand. World of WearableArt is a vibrant multimedia competition established in 1987, which continues to invite entrants from around the world to sew and sculpt their most ambitious garments. Whimsical and technically impressive, many of the works call upon cultural traditions, while others tap into nature, futurism, and the chimerical.
This year’s show is titled GLO!, with Kayla Christensen of New Zealand taking the top prize for her work “Sacred Nightfall,” a spectacularly noble, draped floral garment that nods to Indigenous ceremonial cloaks. Additional standouts include the enigmatic “Enchantress” by Ashish Dhaka and an iridescent insect by Katherine Bertram, among many others. Performances of GLO! continue through October 4 at TBS Arena in Wellington. See more on the program’s site.

title: Tomás Saraceno Returns to the Past to Envision a More Just Future
description: How might we visualize the inextricable web of space, time, and matter, enormous concepts that are so systemic they can almost become abstract? Re
body:
How might we visualize the inextricable web of space, time, and matter, enormous concepts that are so systemic they can almost become abstract? Rendering these connections in a tangible, accessible, and even participatory manner continues to ground Tomás Saraceno’s multidisciplinary practice. Born in Argentina and based in Berlin, the artist plays with scale and spectacle to draw our attention to the life-giving ecosystems in which we’re all bound, merging art, architecture, and science into alluring works.
At Haus der Kunst, Saraceno’s ecological and collaborative projects take center stage for a sweeping presentation titled Ancestral Futures. Spanning more than two decades, the solo exhibition emerges from the central premise that the knowledge we’ve gained in the past is critical to understanding and creating our shared tomorrow. 
Tomás Saraceno in collaboration, ‘Ancestral Futures’ exhibition view at Haus der Kunst München (2026). Photo by Agostino Osio, © Haus der Kunst München
Called “the art world’s favorite arachnophile,” Saraceno frequently returns to the spider and its web as a metaphor for and example of the networks that undergird life. Interactive installations invite visitors to crawl through sprawling structures, while the decade-long Webs of At-tent(s)ion series welcomes several species of spiders into the museum to spin their sticky structures inside boxes. Continually returning to the web is a clear reminder that we’re all connected to one another and that nature’s processes are cyclical.
Saraceno also adapts his interest in solar-powered air balloons for the museum. An immersive cavern made of crowd-sourced plastic bags inflates with the help of willing visitors who ride stationary bicycles to power the project. Others can wander inside, where they become enveloped by a colorful patchwork of brands and remnants of humanity’s culture of disposability and consumerism.
Perhaps the most impressive works in the exhibition are those created as part of Saraceno’s ongoing collaboration with Indigenous communities of Red Atacama, in the basin of Salinas Grandes in northwestern Argentina. Eleven weavers loaned their handmade blankets, which are presented together as a vibrant, soft space for lounging at the show’s opening. Immersion into the landscape of Salinas Grandes follows with galleries filled with sand, water, salt, and more.
Several works reference The Sanctuary of Water, the multi-pronged project Saraceno and the people of Salinas Grandes are undertaking together. The collaboration, the museum says, “emerges in solidarity with the communities’resistance to lithium mining in one of the world’s largest lithium-rich regions. Their struggle highlights the continuing legacy of colonial exploitation: While international corporations profit from resources such as lithium—essential for technologies including electric cars—the environmental and social costs are borne by local communities.”



As a permanent land work, “The Sanctuary of Water” is organized around a large reflective pond that captures the sky above, skewing boundaries between land and air. “In our worldview,” says the collaborative project’s website, “Pacha names the inseparable weave of space, time, and matter. It is one living body, sustained by the water that flows through them all.”
If you’re in Munich, you can see Ancestral Futures through February 7. Otherwise, explore more of the artist’s collaboration with the communities of Salinas Grandes on the project’s website.
“The Sanctuary of Water” (2026). Photo © Studio Tomás Saraceno
Tomás Saraceno in collaboration, ‘Ancestral Futures’ exhibition view at Haus der Kunst München (2026). Photo by Agostino Osio, © Haus der Kunst München
“El Santuario del Agua Salinas Grandes” (2026). Photo © Studio Tomás Saraceno
“When the Llama Drinks from the Stars and the Spider Weaves Cycles of Life, Where the Sky Touches the Earth and Time Expands Like Salt, the Sanctuary of Water Are Fair Clouds on the Horizon” (2025). Photo © Studio Tomás Saraceno

title: In Chicago, teamLab Expands Our Perceptions Through Boundary-Breaking Installations
description: Against a patchwork wall of hammered copper, a black veil appears to billow in mesmerizing motion. The fabric-like layer writhes and twists agains
body:
Against a patchwork wall of hammered copper, a black veil appears to billow in mesmerizing motion. The fabric-like layer writhes and twists against the glimmering backdrop, revealing its diaphanous texture as it unfolds to translucence. Like a curtain flapping in an open window, the digital projection floats across the metallic surface of one of teamLab’s latest works.
Part of teamLab: Everything Exists in Infinite Continuity at the Smart Museum of Art, “Sea of Darkness, Memory Shining from the Depths” is one of several new commissions from the international art collective. Founded by Toshiyuki Inoko in 2001, teamLab consists of hundreds of artists, animators, musicians, mathematicians, developers, engineers, and more who tap into the provocative intersection of art, science, and technology.



The collective has long been interested in the limits of human perception and imagination. Through interactive and immersive installations, they invite viewers into a world where boundaries are suspended and continuity in space and time are key. teamLab was one of the earliest adopters of incorporating digital technologies into experiential works, and they continue to use basic software and programs most people have access to. 
Today, encountering such elegant, yet technologically simple digital works is rare as we witness the exponential rise of AI and a collective outsourcing of much of our lives. In contrast to the tech evangelists and the luddites, teamLab’s approach is decidedly human without eschewing the digital. Works like “Order in Chaos” respond to physical touch, shooting a cacophony of vibrant lines across the floor, walls, and a grid of screens in the gallery. Riotous in energy, the piece “is an attempt to expand painting from a completed image, or a perspective illusion of space, into a spatiotemporal pictorial space that is continuous with the real space,” the collective says.
Bridging divides between time and location also emerges in “Continuous Life and Death at the Now of Eternity II,” which corresponds to its current exhibition’s environment. While on view in Chicago, for example, the floral piece brightens as the sun rises and darkens when it sets. As fall turns to winter, so will the ecosystem on the screen.
Closing the exhibition is one of teamLab’s most ingenious pieces, “The World of Irreversible Change.” Depicting a serene animated community as it goes about its day, the paneled digital work is programmed to respond to human touch by triggering a year-long, irreversible state of war and bloodshed between the inhabitants if the piece is tapped too many times. Several editions of “The World of Irreversible Change” were created, although the iteration on view at the Smart Museum is the only to exist in its original, pristine condition (it’s understandably cordoned off for preservation).



As Inoko tells us during a walkthrough of the exhibition, when the battle breaks out, the community can never return to its quieter days of peace. Eventually, all the people die, and the once thriving metropolis turns desolate. After a few years, shrubs begin to pop up and later still, bird song rings through the skies. But humanity never returns, a poetic if not cautionary tale for our era.
teamLab: Everything Exists in Infinite Continuity is on view through February 21 at the Smart Museum of Art. Explore more of teamLab’s works on its website and YouTube.

title: Wild Hijinx and Hilarious Happenstance Reign in the 2026 Comedy Wildlife Awards
description: The year’s best roundup of the funniest animal photos is back with its list of 2026 finalists, taking on a kind of blooper reel-like quality with
body:
The year’s best roundup of the funniest animal photos is back with its list of 2026 finalists, taking on a kind of blooper reel-like quality with some of the goofiest happenstances and candid moments photographers captured. Nikon Comedy Wildlife Awards 2026 celebrates the wild, wonderful, and wily in habitats around the world.
From Tanner Mansell’s “Spicy Orangutan” snapped in Borneo to a damselfly appearing to wave at British photographer Lee Frost through a window in a nibbled leaf, this year’s top contenders are not only silly, but immanently relatable, illustrating how for all of our differences, we all share this incredible planet.
Tanner Mansell, “Spicy Orangutan”
At more than 10,000 photos, the competition received its highest ever number of entries this year from photographers in 112 countries. “What began as a small effort to raise awareness of wildlife conservation has grown into something far bigger than we ever imagined,” says awards co-founder Tom Sullam. “We use humour to get people to feel empathy towards wildlife, and it’s that empathy that creates behavioural change for the better.”
Nikon will announce the competition winners on December 8. In the meantime, see all 40 finalists, plus portfolios, videos, and youth submissions on the contests’s website. Additionally, cast your vote for the Sterna People’s Choice Award.
